Distinguished co-chairs, Excellencies and colleagues, I deliver this statement on behalf of G4, a reform-oriented group consisting of Brazil, Germany, Japan, and my own country, India. At the outset, I'd like to congratulate the co-chairs, Ambassador Tarek of Kuwait and Ambassador Liese of the Netherlands, on their appointment to this important position. The Group also expresses its sincere appreciation to them for convening the first IGN meeting during the current session. The context of today's meeting is very significant. The world is going through unprecedented times. Challenges of diverse nature are emerging on an almost everyday basis. The universal multilateral organization, the United Nations, is no exception either. The credibility and efficacy of the organization are being called to question. The limitations of the UN in meaningfully addressing raging conflicts across the globe are a driving reason for this phenomenon, although it's a part of much wider power dynamics. Co-chairs, the UN was founded 80 years ago with the hope of maintaining and sustaining peace for humanity. The foundational principle of this organization was clear: maintenance of international peace and security. As a principal organ, the United Nations Security Council was entrusted with this critical responsibility. Therefore, the UN shortcomings in terms of delivering on this vital function are inherently linked to the lack of effectiveness of the Security Council. Against this backdrop, the G4 would like to make the following points. First, the need for reforming the UN Security Council is getting more pronounced by the day. Further delays in implementing timely reforms would result in more human suffering and misery. The ongoing conflicts come at a heavy cost. Countless innocent lives are lost on a daily basis. We do not have the luxury of time to engage in cycles of meetings that are devoid of outcomes. We must collectively make every moment count. Second, the G4 has been consistent and categorical about the essential ingredients for an outcome-centric process. Negotiations on the basis of a text which stipulate clearly laid-out milestones and timelines are central to this. The G4 remains committed to working towards a consolidated model as this could be the precursor for text-based negotiations. Third, the G4's advocacy clearly outlined its vision for a reformed UN Security Council. The size must be increased from the present 15 to 25 or 26 seats. The increase must entail expansion in both permanent and non-permanent categories. Fourth, reflection of contemporary geopolitical realities is a fundamental principle driving the G4 model. Therefore, a reformed UN Security Council must have balanced geographic representation. The means for achieving this is by enhancing the presence of unrepresented and underrepresented regions. Let me elaborate. There must be 6 new permanent members. 2 from the African region, 2 from the Asia-Pacific, 1 from GRULAC, and 1 from VEOG, and 4 or 5 additional non-permanent members, 1 or 2 from Africa, 1 from Asia-Pacific, and 1 each from GRULAC and the EEG. Fifth, our model is aligned with addressing the gross lack of appropriate representation of the Global South on the Security Council. It's based on established norms in the UN. We subscribe to giving due consideration to the case of SIDS for their continued and adequate representation in the non-permanent category. Proposals to introduce new parameters such as religious affiliation run counter to established UN practice and add considerable complexity to an already difficult discussion. Sixth, Our support for unrepresented and underrepresented regions is clear and firm. G4 has specified its formula to address the historical injustices against Africa. This is distinct from general calls without specifics and references to their presence in the permanent category in a reformed UN Security Council. As we have said in the past, one cannot say they support addressing such injustices and at the same time oppose the expansion in the permanent category. We will tackle the problem for real if and only if states from unrepresented regions are elected for permanent seats. Finally, it is the earnest wish of G4 to see tangible progress during the current session. For decades, status quos have been posing hurdles and impeding forward movement. In so doing, they contribute to the failure of the Security Council that, as I have stated earlier, help fuel serious questioning of the legitimacy and credibility of this organization. Groups and member states inclined on achieving real reforms need to come together and resist these efforts. I thank you, co-chairs.

Thank you very much, co-chair. Congratulations on your reappointment. Over time, broad convergence has emerged that Council reform must make the Council more equitable, representative, democratic and accountable, consistent with the UN Charter, particularly the principle of sovereign equality. There is also agreement that the IGN remains the sole mechanism for this process, and any outcome must be based on the widest possible agreement, that is consensus, as mandated by GA Resolution 5330 and Decision 62557. Let us be clear. Security Council reform is not about power. It is about legitimacy. Not about entrenching privilege, but correcting inequalities. Reform that freezes the 1945 power structures will weaken the UN. Any reform that further aggravates the problems emanating from that power structure will run counter to the objective and principles of reform. Only a reform that democratizes decision-making and enhances accountability will strengthen it. All 5 clusters are inseparably linked and must advance together as a single integrated package. On categories of membership, our position is principled and consistent. Pakistan opposes the creation of new permanent seats under any formulation. Permanency is anachronistic, exclusionary, and inconsistent with sovereign equality. It would entrench paralysis and privilege. Any such proposal is also inconsistent with Article 2 of the Charter, and at a moment when multilateralism is already under acute stress, we must not undermine the very principles on which this organization was founded. Pakistan also reiterates its longstanding opposition to the veto as incompatible with transparency, accountability, and collective responsibility. If the veto continues to exist, it must not be extended to any new members. Reform should aim towards restraint and the eventual abolition of the veto, not its normalization or expansion. Regarding regional representation, no single state can claim to represent an entire region. We support redressing the historic injustice against Africa. At the same time, we must recognize. That other regions and groups including Asia, Latin America, the Arab Group, SIDS, and the OIC also remain underrepresented. In conclusion, reform must unite, not divide the membership. It must be driven by collective aspirations, not narrow ambitions; by dialogue, not pressure; by consensus, not artificial timelines. We can only begin discussions on a so-called consolidated model or commence text-based negotiations once convergence has been reached across all the 5 clusters. Pakistan remains ready to engage constructively for a reform that delivers reform for all, privilege for none. Thank you.

To properly reflect today's geopolitical realities and effectively address the growing challenges facing the international community, it is crucial to improve the representation of underrepresented and unrepresented regions and groups such as Asia-Pacific and Latin America and the Caribbean, as stated in the Pacts for the Future. In particular, from an Asia-Pacific perspective, our region remains underrepresented in the Security Council, with only one-fifth of the seats— only one permanent seat and 2 non-permanent seats— even though our region has 54 member states in the UN and contains more than half of the world's It should be highlighted that 53 countries in the Asia-Pacific Group must compete for just 2 seats in order to become a non-permanent Council member, which is the most competitive ratio of all the regional groups. Japan also reiterated the importance of redressing the historical injustice against Africa and expressed our, again, expressed once again its strong support for the common African position. Co-chairs, regarding cross-regional representation, Japan believes the member states should give due consideration to ensuring better representation for small and medium-sized member states, including seats. At the same time, issues such as the definition or appropriate scope and membership of each The question of how to define a cross-regional group and how to deal with the overlap between regional and cross-regional groups require further discussion. We are more than willing to engage on these matters. The IGN session is a particularly important milestone, as it commemorates the 80th anniversary of the founding of the UN. It is in the interest of all those who support reform to move concrete discussion on a consolidated model and to start text-based negotiations. Japan reiterates its commitment to continue to contribute constructively to this end. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Japan for his statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of China.

Co-chairs, China welcomes this first IGN meeting on Security Council reform during the current session of the General Assembly. We expect that under the co-chairs' leadership, members will engage in candid exchanges, build consensus, and jointly advance the reform process along the right track. China will render its full support to Ambassador Albani and Ambassador Van Haren in their work. China supports necessary and reasonable reforms of the Council to enhance its authority and efficiency and better respond to crises and challenges. The only correct direction of the reform must be to effectively increase the representation and voice of developing countries. The historical injustice suffered by Africa must be rectified and special arrangements be made to meet Africa's aspirations as a priority. The 5 clusters of issues are foundational and critical issues describing GATT's Decision 62557 and must be tackled through a package solution. China has on many occasions elaborated its positions on these 5 clusters. In recent years, enhancing the representation of cross-regional groups such as Arab states and small island developing countries has been incorporated into the Pact for the Future and the co-chairs' elements paper as a consensus among member states. This demonstrates that the approach of securing seats for entire cross-regional groups rather than for specific countries, is more fair and democratic and has broader support. At the same time, more and more countries oppose the practice of one election for an indefinite life term and are open to establishing regional and rotating seats. China hopes that the current IGN session will engage in in-depth discussions around these new reform concepts. The Security Council is the core of the international collective security mechanism. It has a special important mission in upholding the postwar international order and safeguarding international peace and security. 80 years ago, in January 1946, the International Military Tribunal for the Far East was formally convened. The Tokyo Trial severely punished Japanese war criminals, upheld international justice, and defended human dignity. It was also a stern warning against any illegal attempt To revive militarism, aggression, and expansion. Yet Japanese militarism has not been thoroughly eradicated. It has mutated and grown in the shadows instead. Japanese right-wing forces have vigorously whitewashed their history of aggression, manifestly denying historical crimes of the Nanjing Massacre, forced recruitment of comfort women, and forced labor of civilians. They have pushed to revise history textbooks in an attempt to revise or rewrite their history of aggression. Several current Japanese leaders have paid homage at Yasukuni Shrine, a spiritual symbol of militarism, showing reverence for Class A war criminals. From Japanese Prime Minister Sannita Keishisei's erroneous remarks on Taiwan and threatening the use of force against China, to senior Japanese officials openly advocating for possessing nuclear weapons, to pushing to revise the 3 security documents and clamoring to amend the 3 non-nuclear principles. These actions fully expose the sinister intentions of Japanese right-wing forces to promote remilitarization and attempt to revive militarization— militarism, posing new threats to regional and global peace and security. A country that shows no remorse for its historical crimes, that violates basic norms of international relations, that challenges the outcome of World War II and blatantly tramples upon the postwar international order cannot shoulder the responsibility of safeguarding international peace and security, cannot gain the trust of the international community, and it has fundamentally no qualifications to seek a permanent membership on the Security Council. China, as a permanent Council member and a responsible major power, stands ready to work with all peace-loving nations and peoples to resolutely defend the victorious outcome of World War II and postwar international order, jointly uphold the Security Council authority and unity, and play a constructive role in international peace and security. Thank you, co-chairs.
I'd like to thank the distinguished representative of China for his statement, and I'd like to give the floor to the distinguished representative of Mexico.

Go facilitators. Mexico aligns itself with the statement delivered by Italy on behalf of the Uniting for Consensus movement, and we would like to express the following in our national capacity. My country reiterates its statements in previous cycles of the intergovernmental negotiations on the 5 clusters of Security Council reform. And in the purposes of— for the purposes of time, I will make the following brief comments now. In the category of membership, one area of reform which enjoys tangible convergence of views is the need to expand the Security Council's composition in the category of non-permanent members. Indeed, there is no negotiating group region or state that is opposed to this. Mexico and Uniting for Consensus have proposed an expansion solely in the pre-existing category of elected members, with the possibility for some of the new elected members to keep their seats for 4 years rather than 2 and to be eligible for immediate reelection. As we have previously explained, As expressed, this would not be a new or third category, rather a different term length within the same category of non-permanent members that already exists. 2, on the issue of the veto. Mexico has historically been one of the countries that has been most vocal against this prerogative since the establishment of organization. Despite that, we recognize that to move ahead in Security Council reform, a proposal to abolish the veto at the moment would not be realistic given the current circumstances. For this reason, one alternative that is realistic is to limit the veto, particularly in circumstances such as when mass atrocities or war crimes are committed. It is vital that our discussions be focused on pragmatic, feasible proposals that can be accepted by all members, particularly the 5 permanent members. On regional representation now, Mexico believes it's essential to remedy the lack of equitable representation on the Council, particularly for developing countries and small island developing states. That is why Mexico's model and the model of uniting for consensus include a rotating seat. On the size of the council and working methods, Mexico's proposal contains a council of 25 members in total, doubling from 10 to 20 elected members and keeping the current 5 permanent members. We believe that this is the right On the General Assembly now, the Security Council's relationship here should be one of cooperation and accountability. Mexico suggests strengthening this relationship through mechanisms for periodic election of Security Council members. Those that aspire to join the Council as elected members should continue to be assessed and elected on their merits and their current contributions. to the international community and not on the basis of so-called historic status. Thank you.
I'd like to thank the distinguished representative of Mexico for her statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Malta.

Thank you, distinguished co-chairs. Malta thanks you for convening this meeting and also extended appreciation for your leadership. We fully support the Uniting for Consensus statement delivered at this session, and we are making the following remarks in our national capacity. Colleagues, reforms of the Security— reform of the Security Council that moves toward greater transparency, accountability, and effectiveness has perhaps never been more important, and, and it is up to all of us to ensure that this IGN is not a wasted opportunity. To achieve progress on each cluster. On the first cluster, many speakers have already advanced criticism of the current structure. Malta believes that the focus must equally be on how we are to expand. And we believe that the greatest consensus exists in favour of expanding the category of non-permanent elected members. As UFC, we've also proposed long-term re-electable seats to strengthen the accountability of elected members. On Cluster 2, many speakers have noted that the use of the veto can hinder the Council's ability to fulfil its mandate. We acknowledge that the issue of eliminating the veto can be divisive, but as a preliminary step, due consideration must be given to measures to limit its use in the most serious circumstances. In this regard, Malta reiterates support for the Franco-Mexican initiative. On Cluster 3, we believe that ensuring greater inclusivity requires additional measures to increase participation from underrepresented regions, in particular Africa, Asia-Pacific, Latin America, and the Caribbean. But it is equally important to ensure representation and address the aspirations of cross-regional groups, including SIDS, Arab states, and others. In this regard, we reiterate the importance of facilitating the inclusion of SIDS in the UNSC's membership, and we continue to support a specific non-permanent seat for SIDS and Small States in a reformed Security Council. Cluster 4 addresses the size of an enlarged Security Council and its working methods. Here, we believe that it is self-evident that a larger Council will need to adapt its working methods, and that as part of this, the distribution of responsibilities among members of a larger group should enable greater participation by elected countries. It is clear that on this issue many individual countries and groups have defined positions, but if we are to meet the aspirations of the people outside of this room for reform, we must understand that no one will obtain 100% of what they want in this negotiation. The times we are working in demand a more flexible approach for us, one that takes into account the idea that reform should benefit the many and not the few. Let us unite around the principles that have attracted the most support, rather than focusing on debates that will lead us to yet another impasse. Thank you.
I'd like to thank the distinguished representative of Malta for for her statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Russian Federation.

Distinguished co-chairs, Russia welcomes the convening of the first informal meeting of the General Assembly within the IGN on the UN Security Council reform. We congratulate the Permanent Representative of the Netherlands, Lies van Haren, and of Kuwait, Tarek Al-Bannaie, congratulate them on their appointment as co-coordinators of this process, and we are committed to achieving fresh results in the negotiations with your effective support. We have consistently emphasized the fact that the Intergovernmental Negotiations Platform is a unique and the only legitimate platform for considering all aspects of Security Council reform. There should be no doubt that the essence here is in gradually building up of elements of convergence in negotiating positions leading toward a compromise universal solution, ideally based on a consensus. Any attempts to force the negotiations by introducing proposals— they are certain to be unacceptable to many— will only set back prospects for a reform solution and do so by many years. The UN would pay far too high a price for such an action. Therefore, results that we all desire must be brought about only through diligent painstaking work based on the interests of all member states. We note that despite criticism of the negotiating process and the disappointment of a number of delegations, the negotiating positions of the main groups are gradually converging, and this is This is largely due to the political will displayed by member states and the skillful leadership on the part of the co-coordinators. At the same time, a universal solution that could satisfy all, or at least almost all, has yet to emerge. Some aspects remain on the IGN agenda where the positions of the main stakeholders still differ from each other, from each other, and sometimes are diametrically opposed. Under these circumstances, we firmly believe that attempts to set artificial timelines for reform or to move the negotiations prematurely to a text-based stage before the necessary conditions have ripened are counterproductive. And we call on all participants to instead focus on the problematic aspects of the process. Distinguished co-coordinators, your practice of examining models of a reformed council has helped identify a number of problem areas in national positions. However, we are convinced that the concepts currently on the table still do not represent the full spectrum of views. And in this regard, we call on those countries of Africa, Asia, and Latin America that have not yet done so to consider presenting their own models that take into account the weaknesses of existing proposals. We hope that such discussions will help us discover common denominators where this is possible. Furthermore, we're convinced that all 5 aspects of the reform must be discussed as an inseparable package. Any attempt to pluck out individual clusters risks undermining the package approach which underpins the negotiations. At the same time, we expect that each cluster will receive adequate attention during this session. A decision can only be made on the basis of agreement of all clusters which are elements of the reform. The Russian Federation reaffirms its principled position in favor of making the Council more representative without harming its effectiveness. The optimal size of a reformed Council, in our view, would be in in the low 20s. We are convinced that more radical increases in the Council's size, as is being proposed by some countries, would lead to excessive delays in extension of meetings and complicate an already labor-intensive decision-making process. And these are not the goals that we are, all of us, pursuing. In terms of geographic representation, of course, the absolute priority must be given to increasing the share of developing countries from Africa, Asia, and Latin America in this Security Council. This is a must. Discussions on this have been going on since the start of the negotiations, yet no specific parameters for achieving this goal have been agreed to date. In practical terms, during this session, we propose focusing on reaching a shared understanding that expansion of the Council's membership must not include countries from already overrepresented or sufficiently represented regions. This is in great deal what impacts and undermines the effectiveness of the Council. And these are, in our view, the countries of the Western European and other groups and the Eastern European group, which quite often follow bloc discipline and introduce no added value. Into the work of the Council. Their unjustified numerical advantage is a clear relic of the colonial past, which we must overcome in the reform process. Distinguished co-coordinators, we hope that the upcoming negotiations will contribute to narrowing the differences in the approaches of member states regarding such a complex set of issues. And to this end, we call on all participants participants to act constructively, to demonstrate political will to find reasonable compromises, and to refrain from artificial time pressure and constraints and from promoting proposals that are certain to be divisive. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Russian Federation for his statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Slovenia.

Thank you, Co-Chairs. My delegation wishes you both successful steering of this IGN process. Slovenia supports enlargement of the Council in both categories, with the aim of achieving both better representation and ensuring that the Council reflects historic changes and today's geopolitical realities. At the same time, we believe that the Security Council must remain of a manageable size, or its work will become seriously hampered— unless there are drastic changes to the rules of procedure. Slovenia therefore favours a moderate increase in both categories of membership, alongside relevant changes to the rules of procedure and working methods. The Security Council is an executive body. It must be agile, effective and swift. Co-chairs, Slovenia advocates for a more equitable geographical representation from regional groups. It is clear that both GRULAC and Asia-Pacific groups are underrepresented. We are therefore in favor of a moderate expansion in both groups. We also hold a positive view of the African position and strongly support the allocation of an additional elected seat for the group of Eastern European countries. We remain cautious about the proposal for expansion via cross-regional groups, as it poses a number of questions that require careful consideration. We believe that reaching an agreement under such an approach would become more challenging, as it would first require consensus on which groups would be established and which states would belong to them. Such changes would inevitably have implications for the existing regional groups, including potential shifts in their membership. Furthermore, it remains unclear whether a state could run for elections within the existing geographical group, where we see no compelling reasons to depart the long-established practice, while simultaneously seeking elections through a newly created cross-regional group. We call for a faster and more coherent reform process, one that clearly demonstrates the membership's awareness of contemporary geopolitical realities and its willingness to adapt accordingly. We are more inclined to consider an approach in which each geographical group determines on its own fair and equitable system for selecting candidates, while ensuring that no member state is deprived of the opportunity to serve on the Council. In our view, no situation should arise in which a country is able to stand for election in more than one group simultaneously, or to defer its choice of group in response to other candidacies, as this would unduly place such a country in a privileged position. Striking the right balance between the size and efficiency of the Council is essential. The ability of the Security Council to take timely and effective decisions must remain the central consideration. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Slovenia for her statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative

Distinguished co-chairs, thank you very much. Germany fully aligns itself with the statement delivered by India on behalf of the G4, but allow me to add a few additional points in my national capacity. Today's meeting is yet another in a long series of cluster-based discussions, and while While these exchanges have helped clarify positions, we should be honest: general debates across the 5 clusters are exhausted. So our focus should shift to the concrete reform models presented during the past IGNs and use them as building blocks for a consolidated model. Such a model would not prejudge outcomes, but it would provide a practical framework for bridging positions. The widespread demand from Member States for an expansion in both membership categories is evident, and it was seen again in last week's debates on the priorities of the PGA and the Secretary General. And this must be reflected in any consolidated model that aims to be credible and responsive. Africa's absence from the permanent category is a special case and must be addressed as a matter of priority. But at the same time, other regions, including Latin America and the Asia-Pacific, remain underrepresented or unrepresented as well, and a reform that aspires to be fair and realistic must include all 5 regional groups. Expanding only some regions while excluding others would undermine the legitimacy of the process. More voices at the table must also mean more voices from all regions. We are open to discussing arrangements that strengthen cross-regional representation, including modalities that better reflect Small Island Developing States, because such innovations can add value, particularly in the non-permanent category. However, they cannot substitute for an expansion in the permanent category. To enhance its legitimacy and effectiveness, the Council needs new permanent members as well. The selection of Council members shall pay due regard to their contribution to the maintenance of international peace and security. And more than ever, we need more Council members who are committed to upholding and promoting the rules-based order. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Germany for her statement, and I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Poland.

Distinguished co-chairs, allow me to, at the outset, warmly congratulate you on the continuation and the assumption of your important responsibilities. Poland extends its full support to your leadership, and I am confident that the energy and dedication of yours will lead us to tangible progress in reforming the Security Council. Mindful that we are all well acquainted with one another's established positions, and that we will engage in greater depth on the 5 clusters later in the course of the AGM, I will be brief today. Distinguished Colleagues, In the Pact for the Future, we agreed on the main parameters of the Security Council reform. There is a broad consensus on the need for the Council to better reflect the composition of the UN membership, as well as for improved regional representation. We all agree that we need to expand the non-permanent elected category. This represents our convergence and it is achievable. In discussing the enlargement, we should also bear in mind that the Eastern European Group has significantly expanded since the establishment of the Council and the end of Soviet Union colonialism. Distinguished Co-Chairs, addressing historical injustices is essential for the UN's relevance and credibility. At the same time, we should avoid repeating past mistakes, undemocratic standards, and granting more of extraordinary privileges whose impact extends well beyond the Council itself. How can justice be achieved by spreading further A central element of reform must be the veto. Even a Council whose composition fully reflects today's realities and answers on historical injustices will not be effective if we fail to address the use of the veto. And again, let's focus on achievable objectives, including making use of existing legal frameworks and supporting initiatives aimed at restraining the use of the veto, while refraining from any extension of this privilege. How can we justify expanding some that we have already determined as harmful? Let me conclude by reaffirming our strong commitment to the reform of the Security Council. It is evident that it is unable to fulfil its mandate largely due to misuse of the veto. This is an argument matter. What is at stake, whatever, is that the system can be fixed rather than replaced. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Poland for Thank you, Madam Chair, for her statement, and I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Namibia.

Distinguished co-chairs, allow me to congratulate you on your appointment to lead the IGN process during this session and to thank you for convening this timely meeting during the 80th session of the General Assembly, building on the work undertaken during the 79th session. This discussion is taking place at a time when the multilateral system is under threat, threatening the very existence of this organization which has kept the world together for the past 80 years. This makes the reform of the Security Council more relevant than ever before in order to make it more representative and more effective. With gratitude, the immense support from all interest groups for the common African position, which culminated in the recognition of Africa as a priority and special case in the reform process, as reflected in the outcome documents of the relevant United Nations processes, including the Pact for the Future. The Pact for the Future has provided guidance We have made significant progress on the way forward towards a consolidated model, and our deliberations here today should encourage such a move to ensure that momentum is created around the reform of the United Nations Security Council. As Africa prepares to submit the African model on the UN Security Council reform, we call on the P5 members of the Security Council to expressly lend their support. Africa is not asking for handouts. We are demanding our rightful place in the Council that is tasked with the maintenance of international peace and security, a matter that greatly concerns us, our children, and our children's children. The reform process of the Council should be undertaken to recognize the need for a more just and equitable geographic representation which should include Latin America and the Caribbean and the Asia-Pacific region. We believe that today's meeting will contribute to moving towards reaching a consensus that would lead to the beginning of text-based negotiations on the reform process. Finally, Namibia aligns itself with the statement delivered by Sierra Leone on behalf of the Africa Group. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Namibia, and I give the floor now to the distinguished representative of Singapore.

Good morning, co-chairs. As this is our very first meeting, please allow me to congratulate our 2 wonderful co-chairs for their courage and for their commitment. to lead this very important intergovernmental multilateral negotiating process, and I assure both of you Singapore's full support. Co-chairs, the IGN process has made some progress and built some areas of convergence thanks to your work as co-chairs, but also the work of your predecessors. We are meeting today and the fact is that we are faced with turbulence and great power rivalry and unilateral exercise of power, but we have no alternative but to press on with this process and build on the areas of convergence. The UN and multilateral system are being challenged and severely tested. In such a context, the need for reform has become even more urgent and necessary to protect and strengthen the multilateral system. Singapore has taken a consistent position that the composition of the Council must reflect the diversity of the UN membership and reflect current realities in order to be credible and have legitimacy. We have also expressed our support for an expansion in both categories of membership, permanent and non-permanent. We will also, as a delegation, keep an open mind and take a pragmatic approach as we review all the different models. In particular, we will focus on how the models contribute to inclusivity and representativeness. In this regard, please allow me to make a few points. First, any reform exercise must address the perspectives and aspirations of small states who represent the large majority of UN membership. No reform model would be credible if it does not make a reference to the representation of small states, especially small states from underrepresented regions or regional groups that do not practice sub-regional rotation. We welcome and endorse the idea of an additional cross-regional rotating seat for SIDS. This is a good step forward, but we think that we need to go further. Only one extra seat for SIDS when more than 50 small states have never served in the Council is not reasonable nor credible. We do not have a specific proposal at this stage in terms of numbers or models. Our requirement at this stage is that small states have to be much more equitably represented in any reformed Council, and that would be the criteria against which we will assess all models. Secondly, priority must also go towards addressing the historical underrepresentation of Africa and other regions. My own region, the Asia-Pacific region, one of the UN's largest and most diverse groups, is also proportionately underrepresented on the Council, and representation across the regional groups must be fair and equitable, and no single region should be allowed to dominate the Council. Thirdly, reform is not only about improving the representativeness of the Council but enhancing its performance. A reformed Council must operate within certain parameters that reinforce respect for international law and adherence to the UN Charter. We believe that there is a need for safeguards that will strengthen the accountability of all members of the Council especially the permanent members. We have previously suggested the idea of a declaration of responsibilities for both existing and potential members to meet this objective of enhancing accountability. This has to be, in our view, part of any agreed package of reforms to be eventually adopted. Singapore stands ready to continue engaging constructively with all member states, and we thank you for your leadership.
I thank the distinguished representative of Singapore for his statement, and I give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Philippines.

Thank you very much, co-chairs. The Philippines wishes to thank you for convening the first plenary meeting of the IGN during this session. We also appreciate the co-chairs' continued commitment to open dialogue, including through last month's informal discussions, which provided fresh impetus and practical avenues for engagement. We meet today with renewed urgency. A Security Council basically rooted in a post-World War II structure needs to adapt further in order to respond more effectively to the many challenges of our era. The Philippines thus reiterates its support for a comprehensive reform package whose elements would consist of both increased membership the Council and working methods aimed at, among others, enhancing the transparency of the decision-making processes of the Council. In other words, a package containing elements from all the clusters. In this regard, we reaffirm our support for expanding the Council's membership on the basis of more balanced geographic representation in order to address, in particular, the underrepresentation of Africa. Latin America and the Caribbean, and the Asia-Pacific regions' representation should also be increased. Achieving this would not only be a matter of equity but also essential in enhancing the Council's effectiveness and accountability in fulfilling, as stated in the UN Charter, its primary responsibility of maintaining international peace and security on behalf of the Member States of the UN. While views remain divided on the veto issue, the Philippines maintains that this issue should form part of any serious discussion on UN Security Council reform. We also strongly reiterate the urgent need to improve the Council's working methods. Greater transparency and more predictability in its decision-making processes— for example, through more inclusive consultations and a fairer distribution of responsibilities such as penholderships and subsidiary body chairmanships— are all reform measures that can be adopted by the Council without recourse to amending the UN Charter. These are just some practical steps that would make the Council more accessible, responsible, and connected to the wider UN membership. We note the revised Co-Chairs' Elements Paper. We thank you for it, and we consider it a helpful reference point. We believe the time has come to move the IGN process forward across the 5 clusters. Distinguished co-chairs, in conclusion, the Philippines is deeply committed to the objectives of making the Council more, more representative and more responsive to the concerns of the general membership. Based on the Philippines' past and ongoing contributions to the work of the UN, we shall endeavor with all delegations in seeking to achieve these objectives. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Philippines, and I give the floor now to the distinguished representative of Cuba.

Thank you very much, co-chairs. We're grateful for the convening of this meeting. Allow me to begin by congratulating you on your appointment as co-chairs of the intergovernmental negotiations on Security Council reform at the 80th session of the General Assembly. We wish you every success as you carry out your role, and we convey to you our full support in this important process. Co-chairs, the necessary reform of the Security Council requires real political will that would be— appears not to be present following a statement that we've heard from a permanent member of this body this morning. Cuba believes that to move towards a comprehensive Security Council reform, including one of its working methods, we firstly need transparent informal negotiations, the adoption of its rules of procedure, which to date continues to be provisional, and that the verbatim reports of closed consultations of the Council be issued, which continue to be the exception and not the practice. The annual report should also be detailed and analytical, which would allow us to address the causes and implications of its discussions. Secondly, Cuba has historically advocated for the expansion of the Security Council in both categories of membership, permanent and non-permanent, in order to forge a more balanced composition. We should have at least 26 members, including an increase of new permanent members, at least 2 countries from Africa, 2 developing countries from Asia, and 2 from Latin America and the Caribbean, so that they can be involved in the relevant decisions taken by the Council. On the category of non-permanent members, this should be expanded at least until— to 15 members. This expansion should not be partial or selective, nor should it involve an increase of Security Council members that would run counter to to developing countries. We are not in favor of creating new categories or subcategories of members because that would entrench existing differences and would foster division within the Security Council. Thirdly, Cuba has always stood opposed to the existence of the veto. However, while this is not eliminated, new posts that are established within permanent membership should at least have the same prerogatives and rights as the current members Including the veto right. We shouldn't establish selective or discriminatory criteria in this sense. Finally, we must stop the Security Council's interference in areas outside its remit, particularly those that fall under the mandate of the General Assembly. The functions and mandates established in the Charter of the United Nations must be respected. You can count on the support of our delegation to continue to move towards a solution that will enjoy the broadest possible political acceptance of member states and would contribute to making the Security Council a truly transparent, democratic, and representative body. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Cuba for her statement, and I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Liechtenstein.

Thank you very much, Chair, and can I thank you both for taking on this important and difficult role. It is not Thank you, Mr. President. This is not an easy moment to discuss Security Council enlargement, but an important moment for doing so. We are encouraged by the positive start this morning. In particular, we welcome the announcement from the African Group that we will be given an enlargement model by them, which hopefully will enable you to produce a consolidated model as a basis for our negotiations. We have submitted our own model for moderate enlargement a number of years ago. The model simply foresees for the creation of a new category of seats, of seats that are long-term, 8 to 10 years, for example, and immediately renewable. This would enable states to serve permanently on the Security Council if chosen to do so by the membership short of occupying a permanent seat as currently provided for under the UN Charter. In particular, such seats would not be given a veto, as we believe that the presence and the use of the veto has been very detrimental for the effectiveness of the Council, and thus find it very counterintuitive to add new veto powers. We understand, of course, And that this is, while a potential middle ground, also a model that requires compromise from everyone. And the big— we believe political compromise needs to be placed in how we deal with the veto in the future. So such a model should be accompanied by concrete measures that restrict the use of the veto and establish a clear understanding on how the use needs to be limited, namely in particular in a manner that the veto cannot be used contrary to the purposes and principles of the Charter itself. The Code of Conduct of the ACT Group and the French-Mexican initiative are useful measures in this respect, and we also are in And we are encouraged by the fact that the call in the Pact of the Future for the full implementation of Article 27 finds growing support in the membership, and we will move this forward with those interested. Finally, we do believe that a more positive relationship on peace and security matters between the Council and the GA is important, and that while the Council certainly does have primary responsibility under the Charter, the GA has a complementary role as this responsibility is not exclusive, and we look forward to further empowering the GA on matters on peace and security. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Liechtenstein, and I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Thailand.

Mr. President. Co-chairs, first of all, I'd like to express our deep appreciation for— to both of you for convening this very important meeting. Co-chairs, for more than 3 decades, discussions on Security Council reform have produced little progress, largely due to lack of political will for meaningful change. But that reality should not discourage us. Rather, it should compel us to focus our negotiations on areas where concrete and achievable progress is possible. As the 5 clusters are interlinked and nothing is agreed until everything is agreed, we should concentrate on measures that can deliver tangible results. First, improving the Council's working methods is essential to restoring its credibility and effectiveness. More timely and structured coordination with other UN bodies, in line with respective mandates of the General Assembly, COSOC, and the Peacebuilding Commission, would support the Council's work. Thailand believes that strengthened cooperation among UN entities as well as with regional organizations represents practical steps that can be taken without delay. Second, elected members play a vital role in the Council's work. Thailand commends the We also welcome the invaluable contributions of former Council members— Nigeria, Guyana, the Republic of Korea, Slovenia, and Sierra Leone. Their regional perspectives, expertise, and principled engagement have added real value to this Council's work. We also support greater inclusivity co-penholdership arrangements for elected members. These practices should be expanded alongside more timely appointments of chairs of subsidiary bodies. The role of elected members will be even more important in a future enlarged council. And lastly, co-chairs, Thailand supports greater representation of small and the inclusion of small and medium-sized developing countries, including but of course not limited to African member states. An expansion of the Security Council must ensure broader geographical representation, cross-regional balance, and enhanced participation of developing countries in order to better reflect today's global realities. Co-chairs, at a time when the Council's legitimacy and accountability are increasingly questioned, with serious consequences for the United Nations and the multilateral system, reform is more urgent than ever, and Thailand stands ready to work constructively with you and all member states to achieve this goal. I thank the distinguished representative of Thailand for his statement and I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Kenya.

Co-chairs, at the outset, allow me to congratulate both of you on your appointment as co-chairs of the IGN process during this session and in a special way let me join colleagues in welcoming Ambassador Grégory Van Haren, who joins us as co-chair, and to congratulate her on her appointment. We also thank you for convening this meeting and commend you for your astute leadership of the process. Co-chairs, more than 15 years— actually 17— after the launch of the IGN process, the legitimacy deficit that prompted it has deepened and can no longer be deferred. Security Council reform is critical not only for Africa, but for all regions whose peace and security aspirations remain marginalized under the current system. Across all models for the Council's reform presented, there is convergence on one fundamental point, and that is that the Security Council neither reflects contemporary geopolitical realities nor fully commands the legitimacy required to discharge its primary responsibility under Article 24 of the UN Charter. Co-chairs, on the question of regional representation, reform must guarantee permanent representation for Africa, enhanced representation for Latin America and the Caribbean, and the Asia-Pacific through a combination of permanent and non-permanent seats. These regions collectively account for the majority of UN membership and feature most frequently on the Council's agenda. It is also time that Africa's long journey towards dignity and equality in the family of nations came to an end. Africa should have a seat at the head table. The common African position articulated in the Ezulwini Consensus and reaffirmed in the Cité Declaration in this regard is clear, and that is full representation in the Security Council, including at least 2 permanent seats and 5 non-permanent seats with the same rights and privileges as other permanent members. On several occasions, questions on which African states would join the Council have been asked. In offering a response, we maintain that decisions regarding which African countries should occupy these seats remain a matter for Africa to determine through the African Union and our own regional dialogue. On the categories of membership, the question of categories remains a major point of divergence within the IGN process, particularly in the perceived structural inequalities of the non-permanent category and reinforcing of the existing hierarchy permanent arrangement. To bridge the divide brought on by concerns about the expansion of the membership, Kenya encourages a pragmatic path forward through a package-based approach that balances representation with effectiveness, authority with accountability, and ambition with political realism. On the question of veto, no discussion of equitable representation can avoid the question of the use of the veto. While views differ sharply on its future, its selective use has constrained the Council's ability to act in the face of mass atrocities. In this regard, Kenya encourages that the use of veto should be accompanied by political commitments to restraint. On the working methods between— and the relationship between the GA and the Security Council, Kenya supports the need to improve working methods, transparency, and accountability, including enhanced interaction between the Council and the General Assembly, consistent with Article 24, and deeper engagement with regional organizations under Chapter 8. This is an area of convergence for most groupings and delegations. Co-chairs, the Security Council reform is not an end in itself, but a means to restore legitimacy, credibility, and effectiveness to the United Nations. Kenya continues to call for a hybrid negotiation approach that combines text-based negotiation with interactive, consensus-oriented, and open discussions in order to capture the nuanced positions and regional perspectives and prevent further stagnation. Lastly, Kenya stands ready to engage constructively, in good faith, and with flexibility to advance achievable reforms
I thank the distinguished representative of Kenya for her statement, and I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Vietnam.

Distinguished co-chairs, I would like to join other delegations in congratulating you on your appointment as co-chairs of the IGN during the 80th session of the General Assembly. Vietnam stands ready to extend its full support to you and to engage constructively with all Member States to ensure substantive and results-oriented discussions during this session. In a world undergoing rapid and complex transformation, Vietnam remains firmly committed to strengthening the multilateralization— multilateral system, with the United Nations at its center. At the heart of this effort lies the comprehensive reform of the Security Council. After decades of deliberation, we believe the time has come to move beyond procedural exchanges and make tangible progress towards a Council that is more democratic, representative, transparent, and effective, one that is better equipped to address today's evolving peace and security challenges. First and foremost, Vietnam continues to support the expansion of the Council in both permanent and non-permanent categories. In accordance with the principle of equitable geographical representation. Africa and the Asia-Pacific, which together account for more than half of the UN membership, remain significantly underrepresented. This imbalance must be addressed as a matter of priority. We therefore support concrete proposals that reflect this reality and call on the IGN to work toward agreement on a consolidated reform model as a key deliverable. Second, on working methods, we call for practical improvements to enhance the Council's transparency, inclusiveness and effectiveness. This includes more regular and substantive exchanges between the Council members and the wider UN membership, as well as a stronger engagement between the Security Council and the General Assembly, particularly in the consideration of the Council's annual report. Third, the question of the veto remains central to the Council's credibility. Vietnam remains— Vietnam maintains that its use must be carefully reviewed and exercised with restraint and responsibility in line with the purposes and principles of the UN Charter. And lastly, with regards to the IGN process itself, we recognize the progress made in fostering dialogue and promoting convergence. We welcome efforts to build on this foundation and move toward a concrete outcome that can initiate genuine negotiations on Security Council reform. In this context, we look forward to focused discussions across all 5 clusters this year, aimed at narrowing differences. Co-chairs, reform of the Security Council is no longer a question of whether, but of how soon we can deliver. Vietnam stands ready to engage constructively and in good faith to contribute to meaningful and lasting results. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Vietnam, and I'd like to give the floor to the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom.

Thank you, co-chairs. Thank you for convening this meeting, and also thank you for your energy and commitment that you continue to bring to charting a way forward, including through the recent taxil talks, or teaser talks perhaps, going forward. The UK believes the Council must be reformed to make it more representative of the world today. As ever, the UK is supportive of the IGN as the forum in which to make progress on this important issue. We have appreciated the opportunity today to hear updates from other members on the 5 clusters and on representation from Latin America and Asia-Pacific, and we hope that this will bring us closer to text-based negotiations. We share your commitment to making progress. Earlier this week, the UK's Attorney General spoke at an event celebrating 80 years since the first meeting of the General Assembly and first meeting of the Security Council in London alongside the President of the General Assembly and the Secretary-General. He underlined that the UK's— sorry, he underlined the UK's firm conviction that whilst the multilateral system is under greater strain than ever before, as he said, global peace, security, and prosperity depend on a strong United Nations at the heart of that multilateral system. A reformed, more representative Council will be best placed to deliver on those pressing demands. As to how we achieve this, Allow me to reiterate the UK's longstanding position. On categories of membership, the UK supports expansion of the Council in both the permanent and non-permanent categories. This includes permanent African representation, as well as the creation of new permanent seats for Brazil, Germany, India, and Japan. We also support the expansion of the non-permanent category to take the overall size of the Council to the mid-20s. This vision of Council reform is guided by the principles outlined in Article 23 of the Charter. Reform efforts should ensure that the Council remains responsive and effective, and it should deliver a Council more representative of the world it seeks to protect, so that we can all benefit from the perspectives and expertise of a wider range of the UN membership. I turn next to And finally, on the relationship between the Council and the General Assembly, the UK has long noted that these 2 organs have distinct mandates as set out in the UN Charter. It is important that each plays its own distinct, vital role within the system. Co-chairs, the UK remains committed to reforming the Security Council and to making meaningful progress in this session of the General Assembly. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom for his statement, and I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Chile.

Muchas gracias. Thank you very much, Madam Chair. I'd like to thank you for convening this first meeting of the world to further our exchange of information on the reform of the Security Council. We welcome the transparent, direct discussions that are held in this space. This first meeting in 2026 comes at a time that we could define as paradoxical. On the one hand, given the geopolitical tensions and the proliferation of armed conflicts over the last few years, it seems that we stand at a pivotal time where Security Council reform would be more important than ever. As this week, the Security Council Secretary General said, and I said, I quote, he said, the Security Council reform is so important that we need to, if we do not overcome its privileges, run the risk to seeing its failure. We need to take be bold to change. The world isn't waiting for us, and nor should we. But on the other hand, with a drop of realism, it is exactly these times when it seems that it is less likely that the discussions that we're holding today might lead to change in the medium term. And that's not due to a lack of interest or will on the part of the majority of this organization, but rather the lack of political will of those who use the veto as a misunderstood privilege. On the contrary, it erodes the credibility of the entire multilateral system. To conclude, we wish to stress that those of us who believe in and defend multilateralism and its principles are certain that the Security Council should look towards ensuring greater regional representation, legitimacy, and transparency in its decision-making so that it can timely reflect the current geopolitical realities. Along these lines, Chile will continue to call for a Security Council that is more participatory, democratic, efficient, and effective, with clear and predictable methods of work that promotes accountability in line with the decisions that are taken within that body. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Chile for his statement, and I'll give the floor to the distinguished representative of Malaysia.

Thank you, Co-Chairs. Thank you for convening this meeting and for inviting Malaysia to share our views on the matter before us today. Regional and cross-regional membership of the Council enhances the organ's democratic character and strengthens its representativeness, inclusivity, and legitimacy. This principle has been articulated in the Pact for the Future and reflected in Malaysia's consistent position on this issue over the years. Malaysia supports the expansion of a reformed Council to include representatives of regional and cross-regional groupings. Strengthened representation of these groupings ensures that the perspectives of its members are duly reflected, as these groupings are often best placed to understand their own dynamics and priorities, contribute valuable context-specific insights toward peace and stability. To contribute to our discussions today, Malaysia submits the following views for consideration. First, regional and cross-regional representation in a reformed Council should reflect a more equitable geographical distribution. In this context, due consideration should be given to developing countries and within regions with varying levels of development to least developed countries that have yet to serve as members of the Council. Second, with regard to the category of membership, discussions have generally centered on whether regional representation should take the form of permanent or non-permanent seats. Against this backdrop, there is merit in considering a third category of membership, namely semi-permanent members elected for longer terms than the 2 years for non-permanent members but without permanent seats on the Council. Third, efforts to enhance regional and cross-regional representation would be undermined if the veto power remains unreformed. Without addressing this fundamental imbalance in the Council's decision-making structure, even a more inclusive membership would remain vulnerable to the exercise or threat of the veto when regional perspectives diverge from the political interests of veto-wielding members. Malaysia therefore reiterates our call for reform of the veto regime with a view to its eventual abolition so as to enable an expanded and more representative Council to fulfill its purposes effectively. Co-chairs, comprehensive reform of the Council must be accelerated And Malaysia stands ready to play a constructive role in advancing this process. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Malaysia for his statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.

I thank you, the co-chair, for convening the 4th ASEAN Plenary Meeting this year. and I express my full support and trust for your effective and balanced leadership. My delegation would like to clarify its principal position on the reform of the Security Council as follows. First, Security Council should be reformed in the principle of justice, transparency, and accountability. The fundamental reason— current Security Council has repeatedly failed to fulfill its responsibility lies in the unjust and double-standard practice in its activity. The selective application of international law, politicization of the decision, and unequal exercise of power have undermined credibility and effectiveness of the Security Council. Second, Security Council must be reformed to ensure full and equitable representation of developing countries. Current composition of the Security Council no longer reflects realities of today's world, in which developing countries constitute majority of UN membership. This is largely because the Security Council remains essentially frozen in the post-World War II structure, despite profound changes that have since occurred in the geopolitical landscape. As a result, Asia, Africa, and Latin America remain seriously underrepresented. This structural imbalance undermines legitimacy and effectiveness of the Security Council. Therefore, it is essential to expand the number of non-permanent seats on the Security Council. Lastly, my delegation maintains its consistent position that Japan must never be allowed to obtain permanent seats on the Security Council. In the past, Japan invaded many Asian countries and inflicted unspeakable suffering and misery to the people of those countries. During its colonial rule of Korea, Japan forcibly abducted more than 8 million Korean people, massacred over 1 million innocent civilians, and enslaved 200,000 Korean girls as comfort women Japanese Army. A sincere apology and appropriate compensation for victims are essential first steps toward acknowledging past wrongdoings and ensuring that such crimes are never repeated. However, Japan continues to glorify its history of aggression and colonial rule through the distortion and revision of textbooks used in primary and middle schools. while moving towards becoming a military power. This clearly demonstrates that Japan has absolutely no qualification to seek permanent seat on the Security Council. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea for his statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Morocco.

Distinguished co-chairs, my delegation would like to begin by expressing its warm congratulations to the co-chairs of the intergovernmental negotiation process on Security Council reform. That is Ambassador Tarek Albano, Permanent Representative of the State of Kuwait, and Ambassador Lies Gregoire van der Ren, Permanent Representative of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. We thank them for their commitment and their constant efforts to move this essential matter forward. In this regard, my delegation would like to highlight the following. Morocco supports— underscores the importance of having a more effective, inclusive, representative Security Council. We reiterate the call set out in the Ezzelwini Consensus and the Sirt Declaration for an equitable representation for Africa in the 2 categories of membership with at least 2 permanent seats and 5 non-permanent seats. Likewise, we support a permanent seat for the Arab Group with all of the relevant prerogatives and increased representation among non-permanent members. The veto should be extended to all permanent members. Finally, any Security Council reform should also relate to its working methods so as to strengthen transparency and accountability to all member states. Distinguished co-chairs, to conclude, Morocco remains convinced that the current intergovernmental framework should be maintained to guarantee relevant, credible, and future-oriented reform. We reaffirm our determination to work under your leadership in a spirit of cooperation and compromise for ambitious, sustainable Security Council reform that would serve fairer and more inclusive multilateralism. Thank you.
I would like to thank the distinguished representative of Morocco for his statement, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ukraine.

Distinguished co-chairs, distinguished delegates, The delegation of Ukraine expresses its appreciation to the delegations of the State of Kuwait and the Kingdom of the Netherlands for their stewardship of the ongoing intergovernmental negotiations on the increase in the membership of the Security Council and other matters related to the Security Council. Ukraine reiterates its consistent and principled position on issues of equitable and cross-regional representation. My delegation firmly believes that enhancing the representativeness and balance of the Security Council is indispensable to adapting the UN to the geopolitical realities of the 21st century and to restoring confidence in this body responsible for the maintenance of international peace and security. Ukraine attaches equal importance to both key dimensions of the reform: the enlargement of the Security Council and the improvement of its working methods. Our overarching position on enlargement is clear: a reformed Security Council must remain functional, effective and credible, and must be fully capable of discharging its primary responsibility under the Charter. Ensuring balanced representation while at the same time enabling the Security Council to respond to the most pressing threats to international peace and security must remain at the core of our deliberations within the IGN process. Furthermore, Ukraine underscores that any reform of the Security Council must be conducted in full conformity with the principles of the United Nations Charter. Distinguished Chairs, with regard to the enlargement of the Council, Ukraine recognizes the persistent geographical imbalance in its current composition. And supports increased representation of developing countries, in particular from Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean. At the same time, the group of Eastern European states remains one of the most underrepresented regional groups in the Security Council, with only one non-permanent seat allocated to 22 member states. Consequently, a fundamental and longstanding element of Ukraine's position remains unchanged: any increase in the non-permanent Membership of the Security Council must include enhanced representation of the Eastern European group. And our last point. Ukraine stresses that all the deliberations on the enlargement of the Security Council, whether concerning its size or regional representation, risk losing their credibility and relevance if a reformed Council continues to include the Russian Federation. Russia, that has committed the crime of aggression against another member state and keeps committing war crimes and crimes against humanity against the civilian population in Ukraine day and night, does not deserve a permanent seat on the Security Council that it has acquired on the basis of highly questionable legal grounds. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Ukraine for his statement. I now give the floor to the Dominican the distinguished representative of the Dominican Republic as the last speaker for this morning's session.

Excellencies. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, we'd like to thank the co-chairs, Kuwait and the Netherlands, for their leadership and for this meeting on equitable representation in the Security Council and on increasing the number of members and other related matters. The Dominican Republic supports stepping up efforts to move towards a more inclusive, representative, and effective Council reflecting the diversity of today's international community. For this reason, we reiterate our position that it is essential to guarantee equitable geographic representation, particularly for unrepresented and underrepresented regions such as Africa, Asia-Pacific, Latin America, and the Caribbean, both within the permanent and non-permanent permanent categories of membership. In this context, we support the following parts of the CARICOM model, that is the balanced expansion of both categories of membership, the gradual strengthening of the Council's methods of work, and of particular meaning to us, the establishment of a rotating seat for small island developing states. As a developing island state, the Dominican Republic understands firsthand the unique vulnerability that we face, that is climate change as a threat multiplier for our security, challenges to our transnational security, migrant crises, and the disproportionate impacts of distant conflicts on our economies and societies. More than mere observers of international security, SIDS are indeed actors that contribute significantly to regional stability, multilateral cooperation, and to implementing sustainable solutions. We emphatically support the call to explore synergies between the proposals presented by the different groups around this reform. We recognise that there are significant areas of convergence, but we concur with the concern that discussions under the framework of these— this IGN will not meet our expectations until we begin negotiations based on a text with clearly defined milestones and timeframes. These negotiations should also be based around fundamental pillars of focusing on transparency, periodic accountability, and the meaningful participation of non-state members of a reformed council. Also, looking at the veto, any reform should be guided by the principles of the UN Charter, particularly the sovereign equality of states, and should strengthen multilateralism rather than eroding it. The Dominican Republic stands ready to work constructively to achieve tangible, timely, and significant outcomes in this reform process. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of the Dominican Republic for her statement. That means that we have now heard the last speaker for this morning session.
